name: New Cross Gate Cutting
text: Your train passes near New Cross Gate Cutting, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve of more than four hectares beside the line. It is a remnant of the Great North Wood, on the site once known as Hatcham Wood, and deer live there; the London Wildlife Trust manages it and usually opens it only on open days.

name: St James's Church, Bermondsey
text: Your train passes near St James's Church, Bermondsey, on the train's {side}, designed by James Savage and consecrated in 1829, one of the churches paid for under the Church Building Acts. Its spire was inspired by Sir Christopher Wren's St Stephen Walbrook, and needed an Act of Parliament of its own in 1831 to borrow more money.

name: Southwark Cathedral
text: Your train passes near Southwark Cathedral, on the train's {side}, a place of Christian worship for more than a thousand years. It became a cathedral only when the Diocese of Southwark was created in 1905, and the building keeps the form of the Gothic church built between 1220 and 1420, though its nave was rebuilt in the late 19th century.

name: London Bridge to Greenwich Railway Viaduct
text: Your train runs along the viaduct of the London and Greenwich Railway, built between 1834 and 1836 and one of the oldest railway viaducts in the world. With 851 semi-circular arches and 27 skew arches or road bridges between London Bridge and Deptford Creek, it is the longest run of arches in Britain.

name: Maltby Street Market
text: Your train passes near Maltby Street Market, on the train's {side}, a weekly street-food and provisions market near Tower Bridge. The street was roughly the site of a ropewalk, in an area once known for making rigging and cable for sailing ships, and the market's yard is still called the Ropewalk.

name: Neckinger Mills
text: Your train passes near Neckinger Mills, on the train's {side}, a warehouse of the tanners Bevington & Sons, completed in 1864 and named after the River Neckinger, which now runs underground. A paper mill stood here before the firm took over the site in 1806.

name: The Den
text: Your train passes near The Den, on the train's {side}, home of Millwall Football Club since 1993, when it replaced the Old Den a quarter of a mile away. It is the sixth ground the club has had since it was formed on the Isle of Dogs in 1885.

name: Peckham Rye station
text: Peckham Rye station, at one end of this stretch, opened on December 1st 1865 and was designed by Charles Henry Driver, the architect of the Abbey Mills and Crossness pumping stations. Its platforms are on two separate viaducts, with a single ticket hall at ground level.

name: New Cross Stadium
text: Your train passes near the site of New Cross Stadium, on the train's {side}, opened on June 1st 1933 for greyhound racing and later used for speedway. Its tight, banked speedway track was known as "The Frying Pan". The stadium closed in 1969 and was demolished in 1975.

name: Canada Water
text: Your train passes near the lake of Canada Water, on the train's {side}, the surviving northern third of Canada Dock, which was mainly used by ships from Canada. After the docks closed in the 1970s, about half of the dock was filled in for the Surrey Quays Shopping Centre, and the rest became a lake and wildlife refuge.

name: Brunel Museum
text: Your train passes near the Brunel Museum, on the train's {side}, in the engine house Marc Brunel designed for the Thames Tunnel. The tunnel's shaft beside it was the world's first caisson: a brick tower 50 feet across, built above ground and then sunk under its own weight.

name: Thames Tunnel
text: Your train runs through the Thames Tunnel, the first tunnel known to have been built successfully under a navigable river. Marc Brunel and his son Isambard built it between 1825 and 1843 for horse-drawn carriages, but it was mostly used by people on foot until it became a railway tunnel in 1869.

name: St George in the East
text: Your train passes near St George in the East, on the train's {side}, one of the six churches Nicholas Hawksmoor designed in London, built from 1714 to 1729. Its walls and distinctive "pepper-pot" towers hold a modern church interior built inside them in 1964.

name: Sanford Housing Co-operative
text: Your train passes near Sanford Housing Co-operative, on the train's {side}, the first purpose-built housing co-operative in the United Kingdom, which has run without a break since it opened in 1974. About 120 people live there, in a street of shared houses and studio flats run by its members.

name: SELCHP
text: Your train passes near SELCHP, on the train's {side}, an energy-from-waste plant that can burn up to 420,000 tonnes of rubbish a year and generate up to 35 megawatts. It grew from Lewisham, Southwark and Greenwich councils coming together in 1986 to find an alternative to landfill.

name: Stone House, Deptford
text: Your train passes near Stone House, on the train's {side}, built between 1771 and 1773 by the architect George Gibson the younger for himself. Its design is so unusual that in the 19th century it was commonly known as the Comical House, and some maps of the time labelled it so.

name: Brookmill Road Local Nature Reserve
text: Your train passes near Brookmill Road Local Nature Reserve, on the train's {side}, on the embankment of a disused railway: its trains stopped in 1916 and the tracks were lifted in 1929. Lewisham Council bought the land in 1979 and made it a nature reserve, with three small ponds.

name: St Paul's, Deptford
text: Your train passes near St Paul's, Deptford, on the train's {side}, designed by Thomas Archer and built between 1712 and 1730. It is one of the 12 churches actually built of the 50 planned by the New Church Commissioners, and the Buildings of England calls it one of the most moving 18th-century churches in London.

name: National Maritime Museum
text: Your train passes near the National Maritime Museum, on the train's {side}, created by an Act of Parliament in 1934 and based largely on gifts from Sir James Caird. King George VI opened it on April 27th 1937.

name: East Greenwich Pleasaunce
text: Your train passes near East Greenwich Pleasaunce, on the train's {side}, a park that was once the graveyard of Greenwich Hospital. When a railway tunnel was built, the remains of about 3,000 sailors and officers, including men who had fought at Trafalgar, were moved here from the hospital's own grounds in 1875.

name: Woodlands House
text: Your train passes near Woodlands House, on the train's {side}, a Georgian villa built from 1774 to 1776 for John Julius Angerstein, whose art collection was bought in 1824 to form the core of the National Gallery. It was designed by the local architect George Gibson and now houses a Steiner school.

name: Kent Championships
text: Your train passes near Beckenham Cricket Club's ground in Foxgrove Road, on the train's {side}, where the Kent Championships, a grass-court tennis tournament, were played in the first half of June from 1886 to 1996.

name: HSBC Sports and Social Club
text: Your train passes near the HSBC Sports and Social Club ground, on the train's {side}, set up in 1920 and known as the Midland Bank Sports Ground until 1992. Kent played a single one-day match there, beating Lancashire in a rain-affected game in 1970, and the River Pool runs along its western edge.

name: Bowie Bandstand
text: Your train passes near the Bowie Bandstand, on the train's {side}, put up in 1905 in Croydon Road Recreation Ground and believed to be the only surviving bandstand by the McCallum and Hope Iron Foundry of Glasgow. On August 16th 1969 David Bowie helped organise, compere and perform at a free festival there.

name: Long Lane Wood
text: Your train passes near Long Lane Wood, on the train's {side}, 15 acres of ancient woodland, mostly English oak with the odd beech. It was part of the Great North Wood, and has a small fenced-off bird sanctuary at the back.

name: Wellcome Research Laboratories
text: Your train passes near the site of the Wellcome Research Laboratories, on the train's {side}. Henry Wellcome bought the 105-acre site in 1919 for £32,000, and its scientists developed the antibiotic trimethoprim; it closed in 1995, after Glaxo took Wellcome over.

name: St Mary the Virgin, Hayes
text: Your train passes near the church of St Mary the Virgin in Hayes, on the train's {side}, built in the 12th century and much enlarged in Victorian times to designs by Sir George Gilbert Scott and his son John Oldrid Scott.

name: County Cricket Ground, Beckenham
text: Your train passes near the County Ground, Beckenham, on the train's {side}, set up by Lloyds Bank in 1918 as its main sports ground near London. It was first used for first-class cricket in 1954, hosted two matches in the 1993 Women's Cricket World Cup, and has been a regular Kent outground since 2003.

name: Private Banks Sports Ground
text: Your train passes near the Private Banks Sports Ground, on the train's {side}, used by Kent for first-class cricket from 1875 to 1921. In 2012 it was sold to the educational foundation of nearby St Dunstan's College and renamed the Jubilee Ground.

name: Alex Yee Ladywell Arena
text: Your train passes near the Alex Yee Ladywell Arena, on the train's {side}, an athletics stadium renamed on November 22nd 2024 after the Olympic triathlete Alex Yee, who trained on its track early in his career. He asked for "Ladywell" to be kept in the name.

name: Bishop Challoner School
text: Your train passes near the former Bishop Challoner School, on the train's {side}, a Roman Catholic independent day school that began as a junior school and added a senior wing in 1956. It closed on July 4th 2025.

name: Bromley Reform Synagogue
text: Your train passes near Bromley Reform Synagogue, on the train's {side}, whose congregation was founded in 1964 and moved here in 1967. Its sanctuary was refurbished in light wood and glass to reflect the community's Hebrew name, Beit Or, House of Light.

name: Beckenham Place Park
text: Your train passes near Beckenham Place Park, on the train's {side}, a large park laid out by John Cator the younger in the second half of the 18th century. Its Palladian mansion, which gave the park its name, is now a community centre and café.

name: Catford Studios
text: Your train passes near the site of Catford Studios, on the train's {side}, a film studio built in 1914. During the First World War it made Tom Brown's Schooldays and The Man Who Bought London, the first film of an Edgar Wallace story, and it closed in 1921.

name: The Fellowship Inn
text: Your train passes near the Fellowship Inn, on the train's {side}, built in 1923 and 1924 as the first pub on a London housing estate. Fleetwood Mac played there, and the boxer Henry Cooper trained and lived there before his 1963 fight against Cassius Clay.

name: Catford Stadium
text: Your train passes near the site of Catford Stadium, on the train's {side}, a greyhound track built in 1932 on Southern Railway land between two commuter lines. At its first meeting, on July 30th 1932, the greyhound Mick the Miller was paraded round the track.

name: Brockley Jack Theatre
text: Your train passes near the Brockley Jack Theatre, on the train's {side}, which shares a building with the Brockley Jack pub. It opened in 1992 with two Chekhov pieces, On the Harmful Effects of Tobacco and Swansong, and puts on new writing as well as established works.

name: Simpson's Manor
text: Your train passes near the site of Simpson's Place, on the train's {side}, a moated medieval manor house; in the reign of Henry V, William Clark asked for a licence to build it with crenellated walls and a deep moat. It was demolished around 1870, and its name lives on in Simpsons Road.

name: St Blaise's Well
text: Your train passes near St Blaise's Well, on the train's {side}, a holy well in the grounds of the old palace of the Bishops of Rochester, now part of Bromley Civic Centre. Its water, with traces of iron, was believed to heal, and it became a place of pilgrimage with an oratory to St Blaise beside it.

name: Chislehurst Junction
text: Your train passes near Chislehurst Junction, on the train's {side}, where the South Eastern and Chatham main lines pass over each other. Loops joining them were built after the two railway companies merged in 1899; the first, the down Bickley Loop, opened on September 8th 1902.
